topics.title: Traders from Europe and the East India Company

learn.hook: European ships sailed for months around Africa to reach India. They came for pepper, cloves and fine cotton cloth, not to rule. So how did one company end up governing India?
points: In 1498, the Portuguese sailor Vasco da Gama reached Calicut (Kozhikode) on the Malabar coast by sailing around Africa. This opened a sea route from Europe to India.
The Portuguese, the Dutch, the English and the French all set up trading companies to buy Indian spices, cotton and silk cloth, and indigo.
The English East India Company was given a royal charter by Queen Elizabeth I in 1600, which gave it the sole right among English merchants to trade with the East.
The Company built trading posts called factories, often protected by forts. Its main centres became Madras (Fort St George), Bombay and Calcutta (Fort William).
The European companies competed fiercely, and the English and French fought each other in south India in the 18th century.

example.q: Think it through: Why did a trading company need forts and soldiers?
steps: The companies were rivals and often attacked each other's ships and posts.
They wanted to protect their warehouses full of goods.
Soldiers and forts also let them put pressure on local rulers.
Over time, this military power turned the Company from a trader into a ruler.
example.answer: To protect goods from rivals, and because armed power let the Company press local rulers; this later helped it take over territory.

learn.reallife: Fort St George in Chennai still stands and houses the Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly. Kozhikode's Kappad beach has a memorial marking Vasco da Gama's landing.

games.title: Arrival timeline
items: Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut (1498)
English East India Company gets its charter (1600)
Battle of Plassey (1757)
Revolt of 1857

quiz.q: Who reached Calicut by sea from Europe in 1498?
quiz.explain: The Portuguese sailor Vasco da Gama opened the sea route to India.
quiz.mistake: Confuses explorers; Columbus reached the Americas

quiz.q: In which year did the English East India Company get its royal charter?
quiz.explain: Queen Elizabeth I granted the charter in 1600.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up key dates of the colonial period

quiz.q: What were the trading posts of European companies called?
quiz.explain: A 'factory' then meant a trading post where agents (factors) stored and traded goods.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a factory always means a place where goods are manufactured

quiz.q: Which goods drew European traders to India?
options: Spices and cotton and silk cloth
quiz.explain: Pepper, cloves, fine cotton and silk cloth were highly prized in Europe.
quiz.mistake: Picks modern goods for an earlier age

quiz.q: Fort William was the Company's fort in:
quiz.explain: Fort William was in Calcutta (Kolkata); Fort St George was in Madras.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the Company's forts

quiz.q: Which European power did the English fight in south India in the 18th century?
quiz.explain: The English and French companies fought several wars for control in the south.
quiz.mistake: Picks a power that was not trading in India then

quiz.q: Which queen gave the English East India Company its charter?
quiz.explain: Elizabeth I granted it in 1600; Victoria became Empress of India much later.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Elizabeth I with Victoria

quiz.q: Calicut, where Vasco da Gama landed, is on the coast of which present-day state?
quiz.explain: Calicut (Kozhikode) is on the Malabar coast of Kerala.
quiz.mistake: Puts the Malabar coast in the wrong place

teach.ask: Gappu thinks the British came to India as kings. Explain how the European traders and the East India Company first arrived.
teach.praise: They came to buy spices and cloth! I didn't know they were shopkeepers first.
teach.nudge: Why did they come? Who came first, and when was the Company started?

learn.hook: In 1757, a battle in a mango grove at Plassey in Bengal changed the course of Indian history. How did a trading company win a kingdom?
points: At the Battle of Plassey in 1757, Robert Clive of the Company defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah, the Nawab of Bengal. Mir Jafar, the Nawab's commander, had secretly sided with the Company.

At the Battle of Buxar in 1764, the Company defeated the combined armies of Mir Qasim, the Nawab of Awadh and the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II. In 1765 it received the Diwani of Bengal, the right to collect revenue.
The Company fought wars with Mysore, ruled by Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan. Tipu died defending Srirangapatna in 1799. It also fought and finally defeated the Marathas by 1818.
Policies such as the Subsidiary Alliance and Lord Dalhousie's Doctrine of Lapse were used to bring more kingdoms under Company control.
Anger built up and in 1857 a great revolt broke out, beginning with sepoys at Meerut on 10 May. After it, the British Crown took over rule from the Company in 1858.

example.q: Think it through: Under the Doctrine of Lapse, a ruler died without a son born to him. What happened to his kingdom, and why did this anger people?
steps: Indian rulers often adopted a son as heir when they had no son of their own.
The Doctrine of Lapse refused to accept an adopted son as heir.
So the kingdom 'lapsed', meaning it was taken over by the Company.
Kingdoms like Satara and Jhansi were taken this way, and rulers and people resented it.
example.answer: The kingdom was taken over by the Company, which angered rulers like Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi.

learn.reallife: Statues, roads and schools across India are named after Rani Lakshmibai and other leaders of the struggle against Company rule.

games.title: How the Company gained power
items: Battle of Plassey (1757)
Battle of Buxar (1764)
Diwani of Bengal (1765)
Tipu Sultan dies at Srirangapatna (1799)
Revolt begins at Meerut (1857)
Crown rule begins (1858)

games.title: Match the person to the event
pairs: Leader of the revolt at Jhansi

quiz.q: Who won the Battle of Plassey in 1757?
options: Robert Clive and the East India Company
quiz.explain: Clive defeated the Nawab of Bengal, helped by Mir Jafar's betrayal.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the Nawab won because he had a bigger army

quiz.q: What did the Company receive in 1765?
options: The Diwani of Bengal (right to collect revenue)
quiz.explain: After Buxar, Shah Alam II granted the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa to the Company.
quiz.mistake: Confuses revenue rights with full kingship

quiz.q: In which year was the Battle of Buxar fought?
quiz.explain: Buxar (1764) came seven years after Plassey.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up Plassey and Buxar

quiz.q: Who was the ruler of Mysore who died fighting the Company in 1799?
quiz.explain: Tipu Sultan died defending his capital Srirangapatna.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Tipu with his father Haidar Ali

quiz.q: The Doctrine of Lapse was introduced by:
quiz.explain: Dalhousie used it to take over kingdoms without a natural male heir.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up Governors-General and their policies

quiz.q: Where did the Revolt of 1857 begin on 10 May?
quiz.explain: Sepoys at Meerut rose first and then marched to Delhi.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it started at Delhi, where the rebels went next

quiz.q: What change came after the Revolt of 1857?
options: The British Crown took over rule of India from the Company
quiz.explain: In 1858 the British Parliament ended Company rule and the Crown ruled directly.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the revolt ended British rule

quiz.q: How many years after Plassey (1757) was the Battle of Buxar (1764)?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts carelessly

teach.ask: Gappu asks, 'How did a company become a ruler?' Explain the key steps to Gappu.
teach.praise: Plassey, Buxar, Diwani, revolt, Crown: I can see the steps now!
teach.nudge: What happened at Plassey and Buxar? And what changed after 1857?

learn.hook: Indian cotton cloth was once wanted all over the world. Yet by the 19th century, many Indian weavers had lost their work. What happened?
points: The British changed land revenue systems. Under the Permanent Settlement of 1793 in Bengal, introduced by Lord Cornwallis, zamindars had to pay a fixed revenue, and peasants were often squeezed hard.
Cheap machine-made cloth from British factories flooded Indian markets, while Indian goods faced high duties in Britain. Many weavers and artisans lost their livelihoods.
Farmers were pushed to grow crops like indigo and cotton for export instead of food. Famines, such as the Bengal famine of 1770, caused terrible suffering.
Dadabhai Naoroji explained the 'drain of wealth': India's wealth flowed to Britain through salaries, profits and payments.

Railways (the first passenger train ran from Bombay to Thane in 1853), telegraph and English education spread, mainly to serve British needs. Indian reformers, newspapers and the new educated class later used these to spread ideas of freedom.

example.q: Think it through: Why did the first railway lines mostly link ports with places where raw materials were produced?
steps: Britain wanted raw cotton, indigo and other goods for its factories.
Trains carried these cheaply from the interior to ports like Bombay and Calcutta.
Ships took them to Britain, and British goods came back to be sold in India.
So railways mainly served colonial trade, though Indians also began to travel and share ideas.
example.answer: They were built mainly to move raw materials to ports and British goods into India, serving colonial trade.

learn.reallife: The handloom weavers of Varanasi, Chanderi and Kanchipuram keep India's great textile tradition alive, and National Handloom Day is celebrated on 7 August.

games.title: Who gained, who lost?
items: Railways linking ports to cotton areas
Machine-made cloth from Britain sold in India
Weavers losing work
Forced indigo cultivation
Fixed revenue demands on peasants
Raw cotton shipped to British mills

games.title: True or false?
items: The Permanent Settlement was introduced in Bengal in 1793.
Lord Cornwallis introduced it, fixing the revenue to be paid by zamindars.
The first passenger train in India ran between Bombay and Thane in 1853.
It ran on 16 April 1853.
Dadabhai Naoroji explained the 'drain of wealth' from India to Britain.
He showed how India's wealth was being sent to Britain.
Colonial rule helped Indian handloom weavers sell more cloth than ever.
Cheap British mill cloth hurt Indian weavers badly.
Indigo was a crop grown for dye.
Indigo produced a blue dye in great demand in Europe.

quiz.q: Who introduced the Permanent Settlement in Bengal in 1793?
quiz.explain: Cornwallis fixed the land revenue that zamindars had to pay.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up British officials and their policies

quiz.q: Why did many Indian weavers lose their work during colonial rule?
options: Cheap machine-made cloth from Britain flooded Indian markets
Weaving was banned by Indian kings
quiz.explain: Factory cloth was cheaper, and Indian cloth faced high duties in Britain.
quiz.mistake: Does not link British factories to the decline of Indian crafts

quiz.q: Who explained the idea of the 'drain of wealth'?
quiz.explain: Naoroji showed how wealth flowed from India to Britain.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up Indian thinkers

quiz.q: Between which places did the first passenger train in India run in 1853?
quiz.explain: The first passenger train ran from Bori Bunder in Bombay to Thane.
quiz.mistake: Guesses big cities without knowing the fact

quiz.q: Indigo was grown mainly to make:
quiz.explain: Indigo plants gave a blue dye prized by European textile makers.
quiz.mistake: Does not know what indigo is

quiz.q: Which famine of the 18th century caused great suffering in Bengal?
quiz.explain: The Bengal famine of 1770 came soon after the Company got the Diwani.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up dates

quiz.q: What was the main purpose of the early railways built by the British?
options: To help Indian kings fight wars
To carry raw materials to ports and British goods inland
quiz.explain: They mainly served British trade, though Indians also used them.
quiz.mistake: Thinks railways were built mainly for Indians' convenience

quiz.q: Which is a balanced statement about English education in colonial India?
options: It had no effect on India
It was only harmful in every way
It served British needs, but educated Indians also used it to spread ideas of reform and freedom
It was meant to free India
quiz.explain: It trained clerks for the British, yet it also helped Indians read about liberty and organise.
quiz.mistake: Sees history as entirely one-sided

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know how British rule changed life for ordinary Indians. Explain some effects to Gappu.
teach.praise: Weavers, farmers, wealth and railways: I see how much changed!
teach.nudge: What happened to weavers and farmers? Where did India's wealth go?
